families.stem: In triangle ${=vs[0]}{=vs[1]}{=vs[2]}$ the right angle is at ${=vs[r]}$. Let $\theta$ be the angle at ${=vs[t]}$. Which of the following correctly names the hypotenuse, the side opposite $\theta$ and the side adjacent to $\theta$?
solution: The hypotenuse is always directly opposite the right angle. The right angle is at ${=vs[r]}$, so the hypotenuse is the side that does not touch ${=vs[r]}$: ${=hyp}$.
The opposite side is directly across from $\theta$, the angle at ${=vs[t]}$. It is the side that does not touch ${=vs[t]}$: ${=opp}$.
The adjacent side is the remaining side. It forms $\theta$ together with the hypotenuse, so it joins ${=vs[r]}$ and ${=vs[t]}$: ${=adj}$.
So the hypotenuse is ${=hyp}$, the opposite side is ${=opp}$ and the adjacent side is ${=adj}$.

families.stem: Triangle ${=vs[0]}{=vs[1]}{=vs[2]}$ has its right angle at ${=vs[r]}$. With respect to the angle at ${=vs[s]}$, the sides are named like this: hypotenuse ${=hyp}$, opposite ${=legs}$, adjacent ${=legw}$. Now let $\theta$ be the angle at ${=vs[w]}$ instead. Which of the following correctly names the sides with respect to this new $\theta$?
solution: The hypotenuse is the side directly opposite the right angle at ${=vs[r]}$. Moving $\theta$ to the other acute angle does not move the right angle, so the hypotenuse is still ${=hyp}$.
The new $\theta$ is the angle at ${=vs[w]}$. The opposite side is directly across from it, the side that does not touch ${=vs[w]}$: ${=legw}$ (it joins ${=vs[r]}$ and ${=vs[s]}$).
The adjacent side is the remaining side. It touches ${=vs[w]}$ and is not the hypotenuse: ${=legs}$ (it joins ${=vs[r]}$ and ${=vs[w]}$).

The two sides other than the hypotenuse have swapped names: ${=legw}$ was adjacent and is now opposite, and ${=legs}$ was opposite and is now adjacent. The correct choice is: hypotenuse ${=hyp}$, opposite ${=legw}$, adjacent ${=legs}$.

families.stem: A right-angled triangle has sides of length ${=L[0]}$ cm, ${=L[1]}$ cm and ${=L[2]}$ cm. The angle $\theta$ is formed by the sides of length ${=P[0]}$ cm and ${=P[1]}$ cm. What is the length of the side opposite $\theta$, in cm?
solution: The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, and in a right-angled triangle it is the longest side. So the hypotenuse is ${=c}$ cm, and the right angle lies between the sides of ${=a}$ cm and ${=b}$ cm.
The angle $\theta$ is formed by the sides of ${=x}$ cm and ${=c}$ cm. One of these is the hypotenuse (${=c}$ cm), so the other one, ${=x}$ cm, is the adjacent side.
The opposite side is the remaining side, the one that does not form $\theta$: ${=y}$ cm.
The side opposite $\theta$ is ${=y}$ cm long.
families.notes: Advanced: the right angle is not given, so the solver must first find the hypotenuse as the longest side (the catalogued hypotenuse-not-longest-side check), then use that theta is formed by the hypotenuse and one leg to name the adjacent leg, and finally the opposite side is the leg left over. Side lengths are Pythagorean triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25) scaled by 1, 2 or 3, so the triangle is genuinely right-angled and all lengths are whole numbers up to 75. Theta is always formed by the hypotenuse and a leg, so it can never be the right angle. Which leg forms theta, the order the three lengths are printed in, and the order the two lengths of theta are printed in all vary, so the longest side does not sit in a fixed position. Answer is the length of the opposite side as a whole number of centimetres. No figure is needed.

families.stem: If $x = {=x}^\circ$ and $y = {=y}^\circ$, use a calculator to determine which one of the following statements is true.
solution: Test each statement by substituting $x = {=x}^\circ$ and $y = {=y}^\circ$ and working out its left-hand side (LHS) and its right-hand side (RHS) on a calculator in degree mode. A statement is true only if the two sides are equal.

$\sin^2 x + \cos^2(90^\circ - y) = 1$: LHS $= \sin^2 {=x}^\circ + \cos^2(90^\circ - {=y}^\circ) = \sin^2 {=x}^\circ + \cos^2 {=90 - y}^\circ \approx {=v1a} + {=v1b} \approx {=v1}$ and RHS $= 1$. The two sides are equal, so this statement is true.
$\sin^2 x + \cos^2 y = 1$: LHS $= \sin^2 {=x}^\circ + \cos^2 {=y}^\circ \approx {=v1a} + {=v2b} \approx {=v2}$ but RHS $= 1$. The two sides are not equal, so this statement is false.

$\cos(x + y) = \cos x + \cos y$: LHS $= \cos({=x}^\circ + {=y}^\circ) = \cos {=x + y}^\circ = 0$ but RHS $= \cos {=x}^\circ + \cos {=y}^\circ \approx {=v3a} + {=v3b} \approx {=v3}$. The two sides are not equal, so this statement is false.

$\sin(90^\circ - x) = \sin x$: LHS $= \sin(90^\circ - {=x}^\circ) = \sin {=90 - x}^\circ \approx {=v4a}$ but RHS $= \sin {=x}^\circ \approx {=v4b}$. The two sides are not equal, so this statement is false.
Only $\sin^2 x + \cos^2(90^\circ - y) = 1$ has two equal sides, so it is the true statement.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Drops the 90 degrees minus from a complementary-angle statement
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student sees sin squared plus cos squared and takes the Pythagorean identity to hold, writing cos^2 y where the true statement needs cos^2(90 - y). They do not substitute both angles, so they never see that the two squared terms are not for the same angle.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Thinks the sine of the complement equals the sine of the angle
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student treats 90 degrees minus x as if it changed nothing, so they accept sin(90 - x) = sin x without evaluating either side. The calculator shows sin(90 - x) equals cos x, which is not sin x unless x is 45 degrees.

The given value $\frac{\{=WCMD[v1]}{{=NUM[v1]}}}{\{=DCMD[v1]}{{=DEN[v1]}}}$ matches only $\{=f1}{=ang}^{\circ}$, so $\theta={=ang}^{\circ}$.
Now find the ratio that was asked for at this angle: $\{=f2}\theta=\{=f2}{=ang}^{\circ}=\frac{\{=WCMD[v2]}{{=NUM[v2]}}}{\{=DCMD[v2]}{{=DEN[v2]}}}$.

So $\{=f2}\theta=\frac{\{=WCMD[v2]}{{=NUM[v2]}}}{\{=DCMD[v2]}{{=DEN[v2]}}}$. The value $\frac{\{=WCMD[v1]}{{=NUM[v1]}}}{\{=DCMD[v1]}{{=DEN[v1]}}}$ belongs to $\{=f1}\theta$, so it is not the value of $\{=f2}\theta$.

families.stem: In the right-angled triangle $ABC$ the right angle is at $B$, $AB = {=p}$, $BC = {=q}$ and $AC = \sqrt{{=N}}$. Let $\theta$ be the angle at $A$. Solve for $\cos{\theta}$ in surd form.
solution: The right angle is at $B$, so $AC$ is the hypotenuse. For the angle $\theta$ at $A$, the side $AB = {=p}$ is the adjacent side.
$\cos{\theta}=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{AB}{AC}$
Substitute the lengths: $\cos{\theta}=\frac{{=p}}{\sqrt{{=N}}}$. This is the answer in surd form.
families.notes: Basic tier: all three sides are given (legs whole numbers, hypotenuse a surd), so the student only has to pick adjacent over hypotenuse and write the fraction. No Pythagoras and no cancelling. The book's figure is replaced by a verbal description with fixed vertex names: right angle at B, theta at A, so AB is adjacent, BC opposite, AC hypotenuse. Legs are drawn from 1..5, coprime and unequal, with p^2+q^2 not a square, which leaves 16 ordered pairs (N in 5, 10, 13, 17, 26, 29, 34, 41; all squarefree). Marker has form null on purpose: 1/sqrt(5) and sqrt(5)/5 are the same number and either is correct. Book model ex5-3-2 (cos theta = 5/(5 sqrt 2) = 1/sqrt 2); note the book's printed solution says 'opposite' where it means 'adjacent'. This family uses the correct word.

families.stem: In the right-angled triangle $ABC$ the right angle is at $B$, $AB = {=k}\sqrt{{=m}}$, $BC = {=k * a}$ and $AC = {=k * c}$. Let $\theta$ be the angle at $A$. Solve for $\tan{\theta}$ in surd form.
solution: For the angle $\theta$ at $A$, the opposite side is $BC = {=k * a}$ and the adjacent side is $AB = {=k}\sqrt{{=m}}$. The hypotenuse $AC$ is not needed for $\tan{\theta}$.
$\tan{\theta}=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{BC}{AB}=\frac{{=k * a}}{{=k}\sqrt{{=m}}}$
Cancel the common factor ${=k}$ in the numerator and the denominator: $\tan{\theta}=\frac{{=a}}{\sqrt{{=m}}}$

families.stem: In the right-angled triangle $ABC$ the right angle is at $B$, $AB = {=Q}\sqrt{{=m}}$ and $BC = {=P}$. Let $\theta$ be the angle at $A$. Solve for $\sin{\theta}$ in surd form.
solution: The hypotenuse $AC$ is not given, so find it with the Theorem of Pythagoras: $AC^2=AB^2+BC^2$.
Simplify the surd: $AC=\sqrt{{=D}}=\sqrt{{=c * c}\times{=r}}={=c}\sqrt{{=r}}$
$\sin{\theta}=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{BC}{AC}=\frac{{=P}}{{=c}\sqrt{{=r}}}$
The whole numbers ${=P}$ and ${=c}$ have the highest common factor ${=g}$. Cancel it: $\sin{\theta}=\frac{{=P // g}}{{=c // g}\sqrt{{=r}}}$
families.notes: Advanced tier, modelled on ex5-8-7 (legs 3 root 3 and 9, hypotenuse 6 root 3, sin = 9/(6 root 3) = 3/(2 root 3)): here the hypotenuse is NOT given, so the student must apply Pythagoras and simplify the surd root(D) = c root r before taking the ratio, then cancel. The book's own triangle is row (9,3,3). Table rows are (BC, Q, m, c, r) with BC = P: AB = Q root m (Q >= 2, so never '1 root m'), AC^2 = Q^2 m + P^2 = c^2 r with r squarefree and r >= 2, c >= 2 (a real simplification), gcd(P, c) >= 2 and c / gcd >= 2 (a real cancellation, and the denominator coefficient never prints as 1). Every row checked by script. 18 stems, answers P/g over (c/g) root r, e.g. 3/(2 root 3), 4/(3 root 2), 5/(2 root 7). families.stem: In the right-angled triangle $ABC$ the right angle is at $B$, $AB = \frac{{=p * a}}{\sqrt{{=m}}}$, $BC = {=a}$ and $AC = \frac{{=c * a}}{\sqrt{{=m}}}$. Let $\theta$ be the angle at $A$. Solve for $\tan{\theta}$ in surd form.
solution: For the angle $\theta$ at $A$, the opposite side is $BC = {=a}$ and the adjacent side is $AB = \frac{{=p * a}}{\sqrt{{=m}}}$. The hypotenuse $AC$ is not needed for $\tan{\theta}$.
$\tan{\theta}=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{{=a}}{\frac{{=p * a}}{\sqrt{{=m}}}}$
Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal: $\tan{\theta}={=a}\times\frac{\sqrt{{=m}}}{{=p * a}}=\frac{{=a}\sqrt{{=m}}}{{=p * a}}$
Cancel the common factor ${=a}$: $\tan{\theta}=\frac{\sqrt{{=m}}}{{=p}}$

params.require: a > 0 and b > 0 and a != b
params.why: the point is in the first quadrant and the angle is never exactly 45 degrees

families.stem: The point $P({=a}, {=b})$ is joined to the origin $O(0, 0)$ by a straight line. Find the angle between the line $OP$ and the $x$-axis. Give your answer in degrees, correct to two decimal places.
solution: Sketch $O(0, 0)$ and $P({=a}, {=b})$ and join them. Drop a perpendicular from $P$ to the $x$-axis, meeting it at $R({=a}, 0)$. Triangle $ORP$ has a right angle at $R$, and the angle we want, $\theta$, is at $O$ between $OP$ and the $x$-axis.
The side opposite $\theta$ is $PR$. It is the distance from $P$ to the $x$-axis, so $PR = {=b}$ units.
The side adjacent to $\theta$ is $OR$. It is the distance from $O$ to $R$ along the $x$-axis, so $OR = {=a}$ units.
Use the tangent ratio: $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{{=b}}{{=a}}$.
Use the calculator to find the angle: $\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{{=b}}{{=a}}\right) = {=ang}^{\circ}$, correct to two decimal places.
Therefore the angle between the line $OP$ and the $x$-axis is ${=ang}^{\circ}$.
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: the book's ex5-8-20 skeleton (draw the right-angled triangle, opposite over adjacent, tan, calculator) with the line starting at the origin, so the adjacent side is just the x-coordinate and no subtraction is needed. The stem and solution are the same for every instance; only the point changes. The calculator has no counterpart in the expression language, so the angle comes from a table of (a, b, angle in hundredths of a degree) computed with atan2 in Python and checked by hand against the book's own 33.69 and 23.96. The table has 24 rows, all with a and b coprime, a != b (no 45 degrees), distinct angles, and a third-and-later-decimal tail at least 0.001 degrees away from a rounding boundary, so there is no ambiguity at 2 decimal places. The answer is formatted exactly from the integer hundredths (fixed(r / 100, 2)), so it keeps a trailing zero where there is one (e.g. 21.80). No mcq: nothing in this family is a natural classification, and the catalogued misconception (a negative coordinate used as a length) cannot arise with a first-quadrant point; it is handled by the advanced family.

params.require: a > 0 and b > 0 and a != b
params.why: a and b are lengths, so P is truly in the second quadrant, and the reference angle is never exactly 45 degrees

families.stem: The point $P(-{=a}, {=b})$ lies in the second quadrant. The line from the origin $O(0, 0)$ to $P$ makes an angle $\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis, measured anticlockwise from the positive $x$-axis (the angle in standard position). Find $\theta$ in degrees, correct to two decimal places.
solution: Sketch $O(0, 0)$ and $P(-{=a}, {=b})$, which lies to the left of the $y$-axis and above the $x$-axis. Drop a perpendicular from $P$ to the $x$-axis, meeting it at $R(-{=a}, 0)$. Triangle $ORP$ has a right angle at $R$. Let $\alpha$ be the angle at $O$ inside this triangle, between $OP$ and the negative $x$-axis.
The side opposite $\alpha$ is $PR$, the distance from $P$ to the $x$-axis, so $PR = {=b}$ units.
The side adjacent to $\alpha$ is $OR$. The $x$-coordinate of $P$ is $-{=a}$, but a length is never negative, so $OR = {=a}$ units.
Use the tangent ratio: $\tan\alpha = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{{=b}}{{=a}}$.
Use the calculator to find the angle: $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{{=b}}{{=a}}\right) = {=alpha}^{\circ}$.

The angle in standard position is measured anticlockwise from the positive $x$-axis. The positive and negative $x$-axis together make a straight line of $180^{\circ}$, so $\theta = 180^{\circ} - \alpha = 180^{\circ} - {=alpha}^{\circ} = {=theta}^{\circ}$.
Therefore the angle in standard position is $\theta = {=theta}^{\circ}$.
families.notes: Advanced: the second-quadrant case named in the objective, and the twist the book itself uses in ex5-8-21, where D(-12, 14) has a negative coordinate that must be taken as a positive distance. Steps: right-angled triangle, take the negative x-coordinate as a positive length, tan, calculator for the acute angle alpha, then subtract from 180 to get the standard-position angle. The stem defines theta precisely (positive x-axis, anticlockwise), so there is one answer. A solver who uses tan^-1(b / -a) gets -alpha, and adding 180 gives the same final answer, so both routes agree. The worked solution states outright that a length is never negative, which targets the catalogued mc:g10m5s8-1-1:negative-coordinate-as-length. It is numeric, so there are no distractors to tag. The calculator has no counterpart in the expression language, so the acute angle comes from a table of (a, b, alpha in hundredths of a degree) computed with atan2 in Python; 24 rows, a and b coprime, a != b, distinct angles, tail at least 0.001 degrees from a rounding boundary. theta is computed exactly as (18000 - r) / 100, which equals 180 minus the rounded alpha, so the solution's arithmetic is true for every instance and is not affected by double rounding. The book's own ex5-8-21 skeleton (two points, angle with the y-axis) is deliberately not reused here: the book prints it as standard tier.

records.notes: Two families, one per listed gap (basic, advanced). The standard tier was not listed as a gap and is already covered by the book's two questions (ex5-8-20 and ex5-8-21), so no standard family was written. Slugs differ in their first six letters (origin / second). Because the expression language has no inverse trig function, both families draw a row from a precomputed table of (a, b, angle in integer hundredths of a degree) and format the answer exactly with fixed(r / 100, 2). The tables were computed with Python atan2 and rows were kept only when the angle is more than 0.001 degrees away from a 2-decimal rounding boundary. The book's own answers (33.69 and 23.96) were re-derived with the same method.

families.stem: $P$ is a point with co-ordinates $({=x}, {=y})$ on a Cartesian plane, and $O$ is the origin. $OP$ forms an angle, $\theta$, measured anticlockwise from the positive $x$-axis. Determine $\text{cosec}\theta$ without using a calculator.
solution: Read off the co-ordinates of $P$ and keep their signs: $x={=x}$ and $y={=y}$. The point lies in quadrant {=q}.

We find $r=OP$ with the theorem of Pythagoras. $r$ is a length, so it is positive in every quadrant: $\begin{aligned}r^{2}&=x^{2}+y^{2}\\&=({=x})^{2}+({=y})^{2}\\&={=r2}\\r&=\sqrt{{=r2}}\end{aligned}$
The reciprocal ratio $\text{cosec}\theta$ is $r$ over $y$: $\begin{aligned}\text{cosec}\theta&=\frac{r}{y}\\&=\frac{\sqrt{{=r2}}}{{=y}}\end{aligned}$
families.notes: Standard tier: the book's ex5-7-1c (B(1;-3), cosec) with the point moved to quadrant II, III or IV so the signs matter, and r an unsimplifiable surd (squarefree, never a perfect square). cosec puts r on top, so the key has no rationalising question: sqrt(r2)/y. |y| >= 2 avoids a denominator of 1 or -1. The stem fixes the angle as measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis (the book's figure shows the reflex angle for B), so the sign of cosec is determined. Instances: 129 distinct points.

solution: Read off the co-ordinates of $P$ and keep their signs: $x={=x}$ and $y={=y}$. The point lies in quadrant {=q}.

We find $r=OP$ with the theorem of Pythagoras. $r$ is a length, so it is positive in every quadrant: $\begin{aligned}r^{2}&=x^{2}+y^{2}\\&=({=x})^{2}+({=y})^{2}\\&={=r2}\\r&=\sqrt{{=r2}}\end{aligned}$
$\sec\theta$ is the reciprocal of $\cos\theta=\frac{x}{r}$, so it is $r$ over $x$ (not $r$ over $y$): $\begin{aligned}\sec\theta&=\frac{r}{x}\\&=\frac{\sqrt{{=r2}}}{{=x}}\end{aligned}$

families.stem: $P$ is a point with co-ordinates $({=x}, {=y})$ on a Cartesian plane, and $O$ is the origin. $OP$ forms an angle, $\theta$, measured anticlockwise from the positive $x$-axis. Without using a calculator, determine the value of $\sin\theta\cos\theta$. Give your answer as a fraction in simplest form.
solution: Read off the co-ordinates of $P$ and keep their signs: $x={=x}$ and $y={=y}$.
We find $r=OP$ with the theorem of Pythagoras. $r$ is a length, so it is positive: $\begin{aligned}r^{2}&=x^{2}+y^{2}\\&=({=x})^{2}+({=y})^{2}\\&={=r2}\\r&=\sqrt{{=r2}}\end{aligned}$
Write each ratio with $x$, $y$ and $r$: $\begin{aligned}\sin\theta&=\frac{y}{r}=\frac{{=y}}{\sqrt{{=r2}}}\\\cos\theta&=\frac{x}{r}=\frac{{=x}}{\sqrt{{=r2}}}\end{aligned}$

Multiply the two ratios. $\sqrt{{=r2}}\times\sqrt{{=r2}}={=r2}$, so the surds disappear: $\begin{aligned}\sin\theta\cos\theta&=\frac{{=y}}{\sqrt{{=r2}}}\times\frac{{=x}}{\sqrt{{=r2}}}\\&=\frac{{=x*y}}{{=r2}}\end{aligned}$
The numerator and the denominator have no common factor, so the fraction is in simplest form: $\sin\theta\cos\theta={=(x*y)/r2}$
families.notes: Advanced tier: the twist of the book's ex5-7-8h (combine two ratios of one point, with r squared giving the whole number r2) but with a product, so the signs of x and y matter and the surd has to be cleared. P may be in any quadrant. gcd(|x|,|y|) = 1 guarantees xy/r2 is already in lowest terms (any prime dividing xy and x^2+y^2 would divide both x and y). r2 is never a perfect square and never has a square factor. The answer is a fraction, so the marker is an expression in simplest form, and the stem says so. Instances: 204 distinct points.
